title: Up to one error
note: The library's reason to exist: a pattern that still matches when the subject is not quite right. Raise the budget to 2 and "collar" is reached as well.
subject: the color of the collar

title: A budget per kind of error
note: Errors are counted separately, so a pattern can allow a substitution without allowing a deletion. Every match reports what it actually spent.
subject: xfoobat

title: Weighted cost, not a count
note: A cost equation prices each kind of error. A kind the equation never names is free, and the weighted total is what has to stay under the limit.
subject: 3oifaowefbaoraofuiebofasebfaobfaorfeoaro

title: The first match the budget allows
note: With an unbounded budget and no ranking, the engine stops at the leftmost thing that fits - six substitutions deep, and not what anyone was looking for. Compare the next two samples on this same subject.
subject: xirefoabralfobarxie

title: BestMatch: the closest fit instead
note: BestMatch keeps looking and returns the cheapest match in the whole subject. Same pattern, same subject, one deletion instead of six substitutions.
subject: xirefoabralfobarxie

title: EnhanceMatch: tighten what was found
note: EnhanceMatch keeps the first match's position and improves its fit there, rather than searching elsewhere: the span shrinks from six characters to three.
subject: xirefoabralfobarxie

title: Fuzzy matching against a word list
note: A named list is a set of literal alternatives supplied beside the pattern. With a budget on top, one pattern fuzzy-matches every word in the list at once.
subject: aple bananna cherry

title: Leftmost-first, as Perl and .NET do it
note: An alternation normally takes the first branch that matches at the leftmost position, however short it is.
subject: abcd

title: POSIX: leftmost-longest
note: The same pattern under POSIX rules takes the longest match at that position, which is what grep and awk do.
subject: abcd

title: Partial: so far, so good
note: The subject ran out before the pattern did. That is how a search box tells a half-typed entry from a wrong one. Finish the date and the match stops being partial.

title: Search from the right
note: The search starts at the end of the subject, so the first match found is the last one in the text. The pattern is not reversed; only the direction of the search is.
subject: one two three

title: Replace with a template
note: Replacement templates speak upstream's language: \1 and \g<name>, not $1. A dollar sign is ordinary text here.
subject: 2026-09 and 1999-12

title: Replace what was only nearly right
note: Replacement and fuzzy matching compose: match the misspelling within a budget, write the correct spelling back.
subject: the color of the collar

title: A pattern that runs out of time
note: Nested unbounded repeats make the search exponential. The engine's own timeout stops it after two seconds and the page says so - and because the engine runs in a Web Worker, the page stays responsive while it happens.
subject: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa

title: Named groups and every capture
note: A repeated group keeps all of its captures, not only the last. That list is what the group table shows under each group.
subject: alpha, beta, gamma

title: Set operations
note: Character sets can be subtracted from one another: word characters that are not digits.
subject: abc123def456

title: Unicode properties
note: A script property matches by what a character is, not by where it sits in an alphabet.
subject: alpha then αβγ then beta

title: Case-insensitive, with a flag
note: Flags are typed by name, so a typo is an error rather than a different set of flags. Try IgnoreCase here, then take it away.
subject: Fuzzy FUZZY fuzzy
